doc.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Brunious family, Creole divisions and origin of the name
summary: Relation to George Brunious and other Brunious musicians, passing for white Creoles, and the French origin of the name from Pau.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: And the Brunious family of musicians?
Is that any relation to your last name?

Yes. George Brunious, Mary Brunious and Abby Brunious and those guys, they were kin to my grandfather but coming from like a Creole family, things were so divided. You know whoever could, we had what we call pasa blanc Creoles, which means we’re white Creoles and there was so much opportunity on that side man. I mean you can’t blame people for just, like I would say if you have caviar here and you’ve got dog food here,

which one do you go for man? So people who could go for caviar went for it, and some of them got away with it and, great. So I mean you can’t really blame anybody for trying to better their own condition.

Brunious. Yeah. Our family came from a city in southern France called Pau. And our original name, Brunoix, B-R-U-N-O-I-X. So then that got to be B-R-U-N-O-I-S. But then it got kind of Americanized, Brunios, and then there were different forms of spellings after that, so that people could pull their magic act let’s call it. So it’s just, things just go like that. And sometimes it’s really tough to talk about because you’ve got people who say oh no, it didn’t go like that because everyone will believe whatever they want to believe and it’s okay. So I try to most of the time avoid stuff like that.
